questions.stem: What does it mean to work in an "environmentally sustainable" way?
options: Using only the newest machines and the most costly products
Using water, energy and materials so that less is wasted
Cleaning faster so that more rooms are done in each shift
Buying everything from overseas so the quality is the same

questions.stem: Which of these is a sustainable habit for a villa housekeeper?
options: Leaving the air conditioning on in empty rooms to keep them cool
Running the washing machine for only two or three towels
Hosing down the patio every morning instead of sweeping it
Switching off lights and fans when leaving an empty room

questions.stem: Why should a villa or hotel care about saving water and energy?
options: It lowers costs and protects Jamaica's natural resources

At midday, when the sun is hottest and the plants are driest

Halogen spotlights
LED bulbs

options: Use a reef-safe sunscreen and put it on before going to the beach
Use as much sunscreen as you can, and then jump straight into the sea

options: Shining bright lights on the beach so people can see the nests

options: Take as much as you like, as the sea brings more each day

questions.stem: Why should rubbish never be left on the beach?
options: It makes the sand much hotter for guests to walk on barefoot
It is only a problem when the beach is a private one

options: They are a good place to dump garden waste

They shelter young fish and feed turtles

questions.stem: Why is buying fruit and vegetables from local Jamaican farmers a sustainable choice?
options: It is fresher, travels a shorter way and supports the community

questions.stem: Which is a good locally made choice for a guest welcome basket?
options: Imported chocolates, each in plastic wrap
Jamaican coffee, local fruit and rum cake
Bottled water shipped in from overseas

questions.stem: Why does the villa manager record the water and electricity meter readings each week?
options: To see how much is used and spot leaks or waste early

options: Take the bulbs out so that nobody can switch them on

questions.topic: Working with guests and the team

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What do the letters NEPA stand for?
accepted: the National Environment and Planning Agency

shortAnswers.stem: What is the small part called that is screwed onto the end of a tap to mix air into the water and cut the flow?
What do we call a shower head made to use less water each minute while still giving a good spray?

Electricity on a bill is counted in units written "kWh". What do the letters kWh stand for?

What one word describes a product that breaks down naturally and safely in soil or water?

Which kind of coastal tree grows with its roots in salty water, protects the shore from storms and shelters young fish?
What floating object is fixed near a reef so that boats can tie up to it instead of dropping an anchor on the coral?

essays.stem: Describe five ways villa staff can save water in the guest rooms, the kitchen, the laundry and the garden.
essays.modelAnswer: In the guest rooms, staff check taps, showers and toilets for drips and leaks and report them at once, because a small drip wastes many litres a day. They follow the towel and linen reuse card, so sheets and towels are changed only when the guest asks or on the set day. In the kitchen, staff wash fruit and dishes in a filled sink or basin, not under a running tap, and run the dishwasher only when it is full. In the laundry, they wash full loads and use the right water level for the load. Outside, they sweep the patio instead of hosing it, water the garden early in the morning or late in the afternoon, and use water from the rainwater tank where the villa has one. Maintenance can also fit low-flow shower heads and tap aerators.
markingPoints: Check for drips and leaks and report them promptly
Follow the towel and linen reuse programme
Kitchen: wash in a basin, not under a running tap; full dishwasher loads only
Laundry: full loads at the right water level
Outside: sweep instead of hosing, water early or late, use rainwater (or fit low-flow fittings)

essays.stem: Explain how villa staff can cut electricity use without making the guests uncomfortable.
essays.modelAnswer: Staff can save electricity in many small ways. Housekeepers switch off lights, fans, TVs and air conditioning in empty rooms, and close doors and windows when the air conditioning is on, so that the cool air stays in. Drawing the curtains in the hottest part of the day keeps the sun out. The air conditioning is set to the moderate temperature the villa's policy gives, not the coldest. Staff use LED bulbs where possible and report faulty equipment, such as a fridge with a torn door seal or an air conditioner that drips, because faulty machines use more power. In the laundry, staff wash full loads and dry linen on a line in the sun when the weather allows. The front desk or butler can explain the energy card to guests in a friendly way. When guests are in the room, staff follow the guests' wishes, so that they stay comfortable.
markingPoints: Switch off lights, fans and equipment in empty rooms
Keep doors and windows closed (curtains drawn) when the air conditioning is on
Set the air conditioning to the policy setting, not the coldest
Use LED bulbs and report faulty equipment
Full laundry loads or line drying, while respecting the guests' comfort and wishes

essays.stem: Describe how to set up and use a waste separation system at a villa, and say what goes into each group.
essays.modelAnswer: First, the team agrees the groups the villa will use, based on what the local collector and recyclers take. Common groups are plastic bottles, glass, cans, paper and cardboard, food and garden waste, general waste, and hazardous items. Each group gets its own bin or box with a clear label in words and a picture, placed where the waste is made, such as the kitchen, the pantry and the pool area. Staff are shown what goes where: rinsed plastic bottles, glass bottles and cans in their own bins; flattened cardboard and clean paper together; peelings, coffee grounds and leaves in the compost; used tissues and dirty wrappers in the general bin. Batteries, chemical containers and used oil are kept apart and sealed for special collection. Bins are emptied and washed often, and a supervisor checks that wrong items are taken out.
markingPoints: Groups chosen to match what the local collectors and recyclers take
Separate bins with clear labels (words and pictures) where the waste is made
Correct examples for recycling: rinsed bottles, glass, cans, flattened cardboard and paper
Food and garden waste to compost; tissues and dirty wrappers to general waste
Hazardous items kept apart and sealed; bins emptied, cleaned and checked

essays.stem: Explain how to handle and get rid of hazardous waste at a villa, such as batteries, used cooking oil, old paint, chemical containers and fluorescent tubes.
essays.modelAnswer: Hazardous waste can harm people, soil and the sea, so it is never put in the general bin, burned, buried or poured into drains, gullies or the sea. Staff first read the label and the safety data sheet, wear gloves, and follow the maker's instructions and the villa's rules. Used batteries have their ends taped and are kept in a closed box. Fluorescent tubes and old energy-saving bulbs are kept whole in a box so that they do not break, because they contain mercury. Used cooking oil is left to cool and poured into a sealed container. Chemical containers keep their labels and lids and are never reused for food or drinks. Old paint keeps its lid on. All of these are stored in a dry, locked, labelled place away from food and children, and are sent to a collector the supervisor has approved. Any spill is reported at once.
markingPoints: Never put in the general bin, burned, buried or poured into drains or the sea
Read the label and SDS, wear gloves, follow the maker's instructions and the villa's rules
Correct handling of at least two items (batteries taped, tubes kept whole, oil cooled and sealed, containers labelled and not reused)
Stored in a dry, locked, labelled place away from food and children
Sent to an approved collector; spills reported

essays.stem: Explain why coral reefs matter to Jamaica's tourism, and describe what villa staff can tell guests so that they protect the reef.
essays.modelAnswer: Coral reefs are made by living animals and take many years to grow. They protect Jamaica's beaches by breaking the waves, which helps stop the sand from washing away, and they are home to the fish that local fishers catch and that guests come to see. Snorkelling, diving and beach holidays bring visitors and jobs, so a damaged reef hurts tourism and the whole community. Villa staff can politely tell guests to look at the coral but not touch it, stand on it or break pieces off, and to keep their fins away from it. Guests should not feed the fish or take shells, starfish or coral home. They should use a reef-safe sunscreen, put it on well before going into the sea, and wear a rash guard. Staff can recommend licensed tour operators who tie up to mooring buoys instead of anchoring on the reef, and remind guests to bring all their rubbish back.
markingPoints: Reefs protect the beaches from waves and erosion
Reefs are home to fish: food, fishing jobs and tourism
Look but do not touch, stand on or take coral; do not feed fish
Reef-safe sunscreen put on before swimming, or a rash guard
Licensed operators who use mooring buoys; take rubbish back

essays.stem: Describe the steps a villa can take to keep its beach clean and safe for turtles and other wildlife.
essays.modelAnswer: Staff can walk the beach every morning with gloves and a bag, picking up plastic, bottles and fishing line, and then sort the rubbish into the right bins. Covered bins near the beach stop rubbish from blowing into the sea. Staff should not rake, dig or drive over places where turtles may nest, and they should report any nest or turtle tracks to the supervisor, who can contact the right authority. In the nesting season, lights that face the beach are switched off, shaded or pointed down at night, because bright lights confuse baby turtles and they crawl away from the sea instead of towards it. Sun loungers, kayaks and other items are put away at night so that they do not block nesting turtles. Guests are asked, politely, not to leave food, plastic or cigarette ends on the sand, and not to take sand or shells away.
markingPoints: Daily beach clean with gloves, and rubbish sorted correctly
Covered bins so rubbish cannot blow into the sea
Do not disturb nests; report nests or tracks
Beach-facing lights off, shaded or pointed down at night in the nesting season
Loungers and equipment cleared at night; guests asked not to litter or take sand and shells

essays.stem: Compare buying from local Jamaican suppliers with buying imported goods. Give the benefits of buying local and the things staff must still check.
essays.modelAnswer: Buying from local Jamaican farmers, fishers and makers has many benefits. The food is fresher because it is picked or caught close by, and it travels a shorter distance, so less fuel is burned and less packaging is used. The money stays in the community and supports local jobs, and guests enjoy real Jamaican food such as ackee, callaloo, local fruit, fresh fish and coffee. Imported goods can be easier to get all year and are the same every time, but they travel a long way, often come wrapped in more plastic and may cost more. When buying local, staff must still check the quality and freshness, that the food is safe and handled cleanly, and that the supplier is reliable and gives receipts. Fish, lobster and conch must not be bought in the closed season or below the legal size. The villa should keep a list of approved local suppliers.
markingPoints: Local food is fresher and travels less: less fuel and packaging
Supports local jobs and the community; guests enjoy Jamaican food
Imports: steady supply, but long transport, more packaging and often higher cost
Still check quality, freshness, food safety, reliability and receipts
Respect closed seasons and legal sizes for seafood; use an approved supplier list

essays.stem: Describe how you would measure and record a villa's water and electricity use, and explain how the records help.
essays.modelAnswer: Each week, on the same day and at about the same time, a staff member reads the water meter and the electricity meter and writes the numbers on a record sheet with the date and their name. Taking last week's reading away from this week's reading gives the amount used that week. The sheet also notes how many guests stayed, because more guests usually means more use. The manager compares the weeks. A sudden rise while the villa is empty may show a leak, such as a toilet that keeps running, or equipment left on. The bills from the water and power companies are kept and checked against the readings. The records help the team find waste early, see whether a change such as LED bulbs has worked, set targets and plan repairs. Staff report any reading that looks wrong.
markingPoints: Read the meters at regular times and record the date, reading and name
Work out the use by taking away the last reading
Compare with the number of guests and with past weeks or bills
Spot leaks or waste from unusual rises
Use the records to check changes, set targets and plan repairs

essays.stem: Explain why staff should report environmental problems such as leaks, spills and overflowing bins, and describe how to report one.
essays.modelAnswer: Small problems can grow into big waste or harm. A dripping tap, a running toilet or a broken pipe wastes water every hour. A faulty air conditioner wastes power. A chemical spill can reach the drains and then the sea, and overflowing bins attract rats, flies and stray dogs. Staff should report a problem as soon as they see it. First, they make the area safe if this is part of their role, for example by putting up a wet-floor sign or keeping people away from a spill. Then they tell the supervisor or fill in the maintenance or incident report, giving the place, what the problem is, when it was found and their name. They do not try repairs they are not trained for. Afterwards they check that it was fixed. Reports also help the villa improve, because managers can see patterns and plan.
markingPoints: Why: problems waste water and energy or harm people and the environment
Make the area safe first, within their role
Report promptly to the supervisor or on the maintenance or incident form
Give the place, the problem, the time and their name
No repairs beyond their training; follow up that it was fixed

essays.topic: Working with guests and the team
essays.stem: Describe how villa staff can encourage guests and co-workers to take part in green practices. Give examples.
essays.modelAnswer: Staff lead by example: they switch off lights, sort waste correctly and save water every day. For guests, the villa can place a short, friendly card in each room that explains the towel reuse programme, asks them to switch off the air conditioning when they go out and gives tips on caring for the reef. Staff can mention these points politely when guests arrive, without forcing anyone. Refillable water jugs instead of plastic bottles, and reusable beach bags, make it easy for guests to help. With co-workers, the supervisor can explain the reasons in team meetings, show the meter records and thank staff when use goes down. Good ideas from staff are welcomed and tried. Clear labels on bins and taps help everyone remember. People join in more willingly when they understand that it protects Jamaica's beaches, water and jobs.
markingPoints: Staff lead by example
A friendly room card or polite word for guests, with no pressure
Make it easy: refillable water, reusable bags, clear labels
Team meetings that explain the reasons, share results and thank staff
Staff ideas welcomed; linked to protecting Jamaica's environment and jobs

practical1.title: Resource-use walk-through and action plan for a villa
practical1.brief: Use the Centre's mock villa (a bedroom, a bathroom, a kitchen area and an outside area). Before you start, the assessor sets up problems such as a tap tagged "dripping", lights and a fan left on in an empty room, the air conditioning on with a window open, mixed rubbish in one bin, a cleaning bottle with no lid near a drain and an outside light on in daylight. As a group, walk through the villa with a check sheet. Each member checks one area, records what they find, takes a safe action where it is part of a housekeeper's role (switch off, close, separate, put the lid on) and writes a maintenance report for anything that needs a repair. Each member also reads one meter (the Centre's meter or a meter card the assessor gives) and records it. Then the group writes an action plan on a poster with at least six actions to save water, energy and waste (what, who, when), and each member presents one action. Photograph each stage below and add the photos, the check sheets, the reports and the plan to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: The Centre's mock villa rooms, set up with the problems by the assessor
A resource-use check sheet for each area, on a clipboard
A meter or meter-reading cards, and a meter record sheet
Flip chart paper or A3 card and markers for the action plan
Disposable gloves and a wet-floor sign
A phone or tablet to take the photos
photos: The group with check sheets before the walk-through
Each problem as it was found (tap, lights, air conditioning and window, bin, chemical bottle)
The same places after the safe action was taken
A meter reading and the record sheet filled in
checklist: Found and recorded the problems in their area on the check sheet
Took safe action only within a housekeeper's role and did not try any repair
Read a meter and recorded the reading, date and name correctly
Wrote a clear maintenance report (place, problem, time, name)
Gave at least one practical idea to cut water, energy or waste, with a reason
Explained their action to the group in plain words
Wore gloves for waste and did not handle the chemical without its label and PPE
Left the area tidy at the end
safety: Do not try to repair taps, wiring or air conditioning: report them
Wear gloves when handling waste, and keep clear of anything sharp
Do not clean up a chemical spill without the label, the SDS and PPE; follow the Centre's spill rules
Put up a wet-floor sign where the floor is wet

practical2.title: Set up a waste separation station and make a guest green-tips card
practical2.brief: As a group, set up a waste separation station for a villa kitchen or pool area, with bins or boxes for plastic bottles, glass, cans, paper and cardboard, food and garden waste (for compost), general waste, and a closed box for hazardous items such as batteries. Make a clear label for each one with words and a picture. The assessor then gives you a bag of clean practice waste (rinsed bottles and cans, paper, cardboard, fruit peel or pictures of it, used batteries in a sealed bag, an empty sealed cooking-oil bottle and similar items, with nothing broken or sharp). Each member sorts part of the bag and explains to the assessor why each item goes where it does. Then, as a group, design a guest card or A4 poster for a Jamaican villa with at least six friendly tips on saving water and energy and caring for reefs and beaches, and a short list of local products the villa could buy. Each member writes at least one tip and presents part of the card. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and the card to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: 6 to 7 bins or strong boxes, and one box with a lid for hazardous items
Card, markers and tape for the labels
A bag of clean practice waste (checked by the assessor: nothing broken or sharp)
A4 or A3 card and coloured pens for the guest card
A phone or tablet to take the photos
photos: The bins set out with their labels
Members sorting the waste (hands and bins only)
Each bin after sorting, showing what is inside
The hazardous box closed and labelled
The finished guest card or poster
The area cleaned up at the end
checklist: Labelled bins clearly, with words and a picture
Put each of their items into the right group
Kept hazardous items apart, sealed and labelled
Explained correctly why each item goes where it does
Wrote at least one correct, polite tip for guests
Spoke clearly when presenting their part of the card
Wore gloves and washed their hands after handling the waste
Helped clean and tidy the area
safety: Wear gloves when handling waste, and wash your hands afterwards
Use only practice waste the assessor has checked: no broken glass or sharp items
Keep batteries in a sealed bag or box
Lift full bins with bent knees and a straight back, and get help with heavy ones
